name: Fermented rice water (sake lees)

lead: Sake lees (sake kasu) is the white pressed residue left after sake is drawn from fermented rice mash, long used in Japanese cooking. In skincare it goes into face masks, creams and bath powder for a brighter, moisturized, more even complexion, and users report a glow after use.

Freeze-dried kasu is reported to contain an extract that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in pigment production, and the masks also carry antioxidants. No clinical trials in the sources reviewed tested it for appearance.

paras: It is used as a mask or cream, or dissolved in a bath, typically on a regular routine and alongside sunscreen. Benefits are described as brightening and softness over repeated use.
Kasu contains alcohol (around 8 percent), and sunscreen is advised for users of the masks. No safety trials in skincare were found.

angle.text: Sake lees is used in J-beauty masks, creams and bath powders for a brighter, moisturized complexion. Users report a glow after use, and laboratory work found it contains a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract, which acts on the enzyme involved in pigment production.

lead: Sake lees, known in Japanese as sake kasu, is the white paste left after fermented rice mash is pressed to make sake. It is used in Japanese cooking and, in skin care, in face masks, bath powders and creams, and in homemade masks mixed with ingredients such as citrus juice, honey, rice water or aloe vera. People use it to aim for brighter, softer and more even-looking skin.

Users quoted on Wikipedia report softer, more moisturised skin, less redness from acne, fainter age spots and tighter pores; proponents credit antioxidants and say it may support collagen, and a folktale of a brewery worker with smooth hands is used in marketing. A laboratory finding that an extract of freeze-dried sake kasu inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in pigment production, is the basis for describing it as a possible brightening or anti-browning ingredient.

Fermented rice water, a related home preparation, is discussed on hair-care forums, and news outlets have covered rice-water toners for hair growth [1][2]. Rice water has been used for centuries by women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia, and Wikipedia reports that Heian-period Japanese women reportedly kept very long hair healthy by soaking it in rice water [3].

paras: During sake brewing, koji mold breaks rice starch into sugar and yeast converts the sugar to alcohol; the mash is pressed to extract sake, leaving the kasu. It contains protein, carbohydrates, fat, B vitamins, fibre, peptides and amino acids, and is part of Japan's "no waste" food culture; one brewer estimated about 250 litres of kasu for every 700 litres of sake.

Kasu is used in cooking as a marinade for fish, vegetables and meat, in pickling (kasuzuke), in soups (kasujiru) and in amazake [4]. Amazake is a sweet Japanese rice drink that comes in two versions, one made with koji and one made with sake kasu [4].

Manufacturers add kasu to facial masks, bath powders and face creams, and homemade masks combine it with citrus juice, honey, rice water, aloe vera or rose water. Wikipedia attributes the reported effects mostly to user reports and notes that, because kasu contains alcohol, sunscreen should be applied before a homemade mask.

Freeze-dried kasu is described as containing a mixture of triacylglycerols with a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract, one of which, trilinolein, appears in some cosmetics, which is why it is considered a possible anti-browning ingredient. A review of amazake lists skin barrier effects among the functions known from research on sake-lees and koji drinks, with the best-studied effect being on bowel movement, in studies using about 100 mL a day [5].

Rice water is a starch suspension made by draining boiled rice or boiling rice until it dissolves [3]. Wikipedia reports that it has been used for centuries for hair by women in China, Japan and Southeast Asia [3]. On T Nation, a user in 2018 said people were "all over" fermented rice water for hair loss, ranking it alongside minoxidil and Monistat as things that actually work [6]. A Hindustan Times headline in 2026 reports that the internet says rice water is effective for hair growth and presents an expert's view on the trending toner [2].

No studies found on topical sake lees or fermented rice water for skin or hair appearance. Related studies of sake lees as a food are a 2025 single-arm trial in eight adults with constipation who consumed 25 or 50 g daily for six weeks [1], and laboratory and animal studies of its effects on tooth-cell mineralisation [7] and bone loss in ovariectomised mice [8].
